chief_complaint: sudden complete unilateral facial paralysis including forehead
hpi_details: A 62-year-old female presents to the clinic with sudden complete unilateral facial paralysis including forehead. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: thinks it might be Bell's palsy
concerns: She is worried that her face will be permanently disfigured and she will never be able to smile normally again.
expectations: She hopes to get an immediate head scan to confirm she didn't have a stroke and medication to reverse the paralysis.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Bell Palsy is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Plan for Bell Palsy: Oral Prednisone, eye patch and artificial tears, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

Key HPI features: A 62-year-old female presents to the clinic with sudden complete unilateral facial paralysis including forehead. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Bell Palsy.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Bell Palsy.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Stroke without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Limb weakness.
management_principles: Plan for Bell Palsy: Oral Prednisone, eye patch and artificial tears
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: sudden complete unilateral facial paralysis including forehead

A 62-year-old female presents to the clinic with sudden complete unilateral facial paralysis including forehead. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Bell Palsy.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Bell Palsy.
reference_soap.plan: Start oral prednisone promptly when appropriate, ideally within 72 hours of onset, after assessing for alternative causes of facial weakness. Protect the cornea with frequent lubricating drops/ointment and eyelid taping or closure at night when eye closure is incomplete; arrange urgent eye assessment for corneal symptoms.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical presentation and diagnostic markers of Bell Palsy
Select appropriate diagnostic workup for Bell Palsy
Implement evidence-based management plan: Oral Prednisone, eye patch and artificial tears

teaching.one_liner: Sudden complete unilateral facial paralysis including the forehead, from HSV reactivation in the facial nerve.

must_ask.say: Can you wrinkle your forehead on that side?

history.answer: Doctor, the right side of my face suddenly went weak, and my eye won't close properly.
It started two days ago when I woke up, and it seemed to peak over about twenty-four hours along with some fatigue.
Yes, the entire right side is affected; I cannot wrinkle my forehead on that side or close my right eye completely.
No, my arms and legs feel completely strong, and I have no weakness or numbness anywhere else.
My speech sounds slightly muffled because my lips won't seal on the right, but my words are clear and my vision is normal.
No, I have not had any severe headache, nausea, vomiting, or confusion.
I noticed a dull, aching soreness right behind my right ear starting about a day before my face drooped.
No, I do not have sharp ear pain, and I have not seen any blisters or rashes in my ear or mouth.
history.topic: Ear blisters and severe ear pain

history.answer: My hearing seems normal, but sudden or loud sounds in my right ear sound unusually harsh and booming.
No, the room has not been spinning, and I do not have ringing in my ears.
Yes, food has tasted strange and dull on the front of my tongue for the past couple of days.
My right eye feels irritated and gritty, and tears keep spilling down my cheek because I cannot blink.
Yes, fluids tend to drip out of the right corner of my mouth, and food gets stuck between my cheek and gums.
I had a mild head cold about ten days ago, but no tick bites, expanding rashes, or shingles.
history.topic: Recent viral infection or tick bite

history.answer: No, I have never had facial weakness before, and the left side of my face feels completely normal.
No, I have not felt any lumps or swellings in front of my ears, under my jaw, or along my neck.
No, I have never had any head injuries, facial trauma, or surgery around my ears or neck.
I have been wondering if this could be Bell's palsy, though I was terrified at first that it was a stroke.
I'm terrified that my face will stay frozen like this forever and I'll never be able to smile again.
I want an urgent brain scan to make sure it's not a stroke, and some medicine to get my face moving again.
I have never had high blood pressure, diabetes, strokes, or any serious chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital admissions.
I do not take any prescription medications, over-the-counter pills, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used tobacco products.
I only drink an occasional glass of wine when out for dinner with friends, maybe once or twice a month.
I work as an elementary school librarian and live with my husband.
There is no history of facial paralysis, early strokes, or brain aneurysms in my family.

exam.finding: Alert, comfortable at rest, with noticeable right facial asymmetry and flattened right nasolabial fold.
Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.6 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Right eye shows incomplete eyelid closure with upward rotation of the eyeball on attempted closure, mild scleral injection, and no corneal ulceration.
External auditory canals and pinnae clear bilaterally with no vesicles, redness, or tympanic membrane effusion.
Normal conversational hearing bilaterally with intact finger rub perception in both ears.
Oral mucosa is moist and pink with no vesicular lesions on the palate or tongue.
No parotid gland enlargement, localized masses, or cervical lymphadenopathy palpated.
Marked right peripheral facial nerve weakness with absent right forehead wrinkling, unable to tightly close right eye, flattened nasolabial fold, and asymmetric smile; other cranial nerves intact.
Full 5/5 motor strength throughout bilateral upper and lower extremities with normal bulk and tone.
Intact and symmetric sensation to light touch and pinprick across all extremities and the face.
Normal finger-to-nose testing, rapid alternating movements, and stable narrow-based gait.
Full active and passive cervical range of motion without nuchal rigidity.
